opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, because in practice people often use the two terms almost interchangeably, and in a narrow technical sense supervised fine-tuning *is* a form of imitation learning. You show the model demonstrations, prompt and response pairs, and train it with a next-token prediction loss to reproduce them. That's behavior cloning, which is the simplest flavor of imitation learning.

But I think it's useful to keep the distinction because the framing changes what questions you ask. When you call it supervised fine-tuning, you're thinking of it as fitting a dataset: you have inputs and labels, you minimize cross-entropy, done. When you call it imitation learning, you inherit decades of thinking from robotics and reinforcement learning about what goes wrong when you just copy an expert. The classic issue is compounding error, or distribution shift. The model is trained on the expert's trajectories, but at inference time it generates its own tokens, drifts into states the expert never visited, and has no idea how to recover. That's exposure bias in the language modeling world, and it's essentially the same problem.

The imitation learning lens also reminds you that copying surface behavior isn't the same as learning the underlying intent. If you fine-tune a model on very polished, confident answers, it may learn the *style* of expertise, the tone and the format, without the competence behind it. That's part of why we see models that sound authoritative while hallucinating. They imitated the form of the demonstration rather than the reasoning that produced it.

So in post-training, I'd say SFT is the mechanism and imitation learning is the conceptual framework. The framework points you toward remedies: interactive approaches where the model learns from its own generations, like DAgger-style corrections, preference learning, or RL with feedback, so the model sees and gets corrected on its own mistakes rather than only ever watching a perfect teacher. Data quality and diversity matter a lot too. A smaller set of carefully constructed demonstrations that cover the kinds of situations the model will actually encounter often beats a huge pile of imitation data.

And there's a deeper point I care about. If all we do is imitate, we're bounded by the demonstrations, and we risk models that are mimics rather than reasoners. The interesting research frontier is how to move beyond pure imitation, so the model develops something closer to an understanding of *why* a response is good, not just *what* a good response looks like.

r001.rationale: The response says supervised fine-tuning is a form of imitation learning and that the terms are often used almost interchangeably; it does not state that they mean the same thing.

r002.rationale: It discusses copying expert trajectories and imitation learning’s connection to reinforcement learning, but does not explain that trajectory training motivates using the term for SFT immediately before or after reinforcement learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think of them as the same mechanism viewed from two different angles, and the distinction is really about where the demonstrations come from and what you believe you're teaching.

Supervised fine-tuning is the engineering description. You have a pretrained model, you have a dataset of prompts paired with target responses, you minimize cross-entropy on the targets. That's it. It's agnostic about who produced those targets or why they're good.

Imitation learning is the framing from the sequential decision-making world. There's an expert policy, you observe its trajectories, and you try to clone its behavior. When you say it that way, you're committing to a claim about the data: these are demonstrations of some competent agent, and the goal is to approximate that agent. In practice, for most of what the community calls SFT today, the expert is either a human annotator or, increasingly, a stronger model. So most SFT is in fact behavior cloning, and I think it's useful to admit that, because behavior cloning has well-known failure modes that the SFT vocabulary tends to hide.

The big one is compounding error, or what the robotics people call covariate shift. You train on the expert's state distribution, but at inference the model's own early mistakes lead it into states the expert never visited, and it has no idea what to do there. In language this shows up as the model confabulating fluently once it's off the rails. The DAgger insight, that you need to collect corrections on the learner's own distribution, is essentially what RL from feedback and on-policy methods are quietly doing for us. So part of why I like the imitation-learning lens is that it predicts exactly why SFT alone plateaus and why you need some on-policy component.

The other thing the framing surfaces is the question of whether imitation is even the right objective. If you're distilling from a stronger model, you're bounded by the teacher, and you're also inheriting its particular style and blind spots. And if the demonstrations are human, there's this interesting mismatch, because the model doesn't have the same knowledge or the same failure modes a human has, so faithfully imitating a human's way of answering can actually teach the model to express confidence it hasn't earned. That's where I think the "small data, high quality" results, LIMA-style, are telling us something. A lot of what SFT does is unlock a format and a persona rather than install new capability, and once you see it as imitation, the question becomes what minimal set of demonstrations gets you that unlock without overfitting to the surface features of the expert.

So the short version: SFT is the loss function, imitation learning is the hypothesis about what the data represents. I find the second more honest, because it tells you what will go wrong.

r001.rationale: The response calls them “the same mechanism viewed from two different angles,” then distinguishes SFT as the loss-function description from imitation learning as a claim about what the data represents.

r002.rationale: It explains that imitation learning observes an expert’s trajectories and tries to clone its behavior, but does not say that this motivates calling SFT imitation learning when it occurs immediately before or after reinforcement learning.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is really about what level of description we’re using. Supervised fine-tuning is a training procedure: you give the model examples of an input and a desired output, and train it to predict that output. Imitation learning describes the objective more broadly: learning to behave like an expert from demonstrations.

So if you fine-tune a language model on demonstrations of good assistant responses, that’s both supervised fine-tuning and a form of imitation learning, often called behavior cloning. They’re not mutually exclusive categories.

But imitation learning can go beyond a fixed dataset. You might let an agent interact with an environment and collect expert corrections on the situations it actually encounters. That matters because once the model makes a mistake, it can end up in situations that weren’t represented in its demonstrations. Simply predicting the expert’s answers on the original training examples doesn’t necessarily teach it how to recover.

r001.rationale: The response says supervised fine-tuning can be a form of imitation learning, but explicitly describes them as different levels of description rather than saying they mean the same thing.

r002.rationale: The response discusses learning from demonstrations and collecting expert corrections, but does not connect example trajectories to calling supervised fine-tuning imitation learning immediately before or after reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is a little blurry, because supervised fine-tuning can itself be a form of imitation learning. When we train a language model on examples of a prompt and a desirable response, we’re teaching it to imitate those responses.

Imitation learning is the broader idea: learning behavior from demonstrations. Supervised fine-tuning is a particular training procedure, typically maximizing the likelihood of the demonstrated response. In that sense, it’s very close to what people call behavioral cloning.

The distinction becomes more meaningful when we consider how the demonstrations are collected. Are we learning from a fixed dataset, or does the learner interact with an environment and receive expert guidance on situations it actually encounters? That matters because a model can make a small mistake, end up in a situation the demonstrations never covered, and then compound that mistake. So I would look at the data collection and learning setup, rather than treating these as two fundamentally separate categories.

r001.rationale: The response says supervised fine-tuning can be a form of imitation learning, but describes imitation learning as broader and SFT as a particular procedure; it does not say they mean the same thing.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning from demonstrations and prompt-response examples, but does not connect example trajectories to calling SFT imitation learning immediately before or after reinforcement learning.
